Critical thinking

Tools to evaluate claims, spot pseudoscience, understand causation and protect yourself from misinformation.

Lesson 2. Correlation and causation

1 · Lesson

That two things go together (correlation) does not mean one causes the other (causation). The relationship may run the other way, a third factor may cause both, or it may be pure coincidence.

The best way to know whether something causes an effect is the experiment and, in health, the randomised controlled trial: people are assigned at random to groups that do or do not receive the treatment, ideally without knowing which group they are in. Randomness makes the groups similar in everything else.

When experiments are not possible, well-conducted observational studies contribute a lot, but their conclusions are more cautious. Be wary of headlines like "people who do X live longer" when the study only observed an association.

2 · Example

In the months when more ice cream is sold there are also more drownings. Ice cream does not cause drowning: a third factor, summer heat, makes people eat more ice cream and swim more.

3 · Activity

Find a health headline of the type "X is linked to Y". Write three possible explanations: X causes Y, Y causes X, and a third factor that causes both.
